teaser.en: Its white powder-puff flowers open only at night, and its light breathing roots have long served fishermen as net floats.

summary.en: The mangrove apple is the tree of the outermost mangrove fringe, standing in open seawater on stout cone-shaped roots. Its wood, bark and even its roots have uses, from canoes and paddles to fishing-net floats.

about.en:
The mangrove apple is a tree of about 10 metres with rounded, rather thick leaves. Around its base rises a forest of stout, cone-shaped breathing roots that poke up out of the mud and water, thicker and taller than those of the grey mangrove.

Its flowers are a sight worth staying late for. They are white powder puffs of long stamens that open at night and are visited by bats and moths, then fall by morning. The fruit that follows is a flattened green berry with the old flower parts still attached, which gives the tree its English name.

where.en: This is the mangrove that faces the sea. It grows on the outermost seaward fringe in normal seawater, where the tide covers it every day; it fringes Sii Island at Vanga. On a boat trip into Gazi Bay or out from Funzi and Vanga, these are the first trees you pass. The breathing roots are best seen at low tide.

uses.en:
The wood is used for canoes, boat ribs, masts and paddles, as well as door and window frames and charcoal. The breathing roots are light and spongy, and fishermen use them as floats for fishing nets.

The bark yields tannin, and the leaves are fed to camels where they are kept.

names.en: No Digo name has been recorded yet. In Swahili it is *mlilana*. In English it is the mangrove apple or white-flowered apple mangrove, and its scientific name is *Sonneratia alba*, where *alba* means white, for the flowers.

conservation.en: It is globally Least Concern, but Kenya's mangroves are heavily cut for poles and fuel; harvesting is licensed by the Kenya Forest Service, and community projects at Gazi, Makongeni and Vanga are restoring mangrove forest.

reason.en: Also grows on the seaward fringe, with pencil-like breathing roots
Stands just behind it in the seaward mangrove
Also used for masts and boat parts
A relative in the same loosestrife family (Lythraceae)
